newsitem.title: USA: Next generation U.S. astronaut heads for Mir.
newsitem.headline: Next generation U.S. astronaut heads for Mir.

text.p: A new breed of astronaut prepared himself on Saturday to blast off aboard shuttle Atlantis for a four-month stay aboard Russia's orbiting Mir space station.
Jerry Linenger and five fellow astronauts were scheduled for a launch from Florida's Kennedy Space Centre at 4:27 a.m. EST (0927 GMT) Sunday, and a linkup with Mir on Tuesday night.
NASA officials said the countdown was proceeding smoothly with no technical problems. Technicians planned to start fuelling the shuttle for launch at about 7 p.m. EST (OOOO GMT).
Forecasters gave Atlantis a 70 percent chance of fair weather during its narrow seven-minute launch window.
Linenger will be the fourth U.S. astronaut to live and work aboard the space station, but he is unlike any of his predecessors.

Those who went before him, astronauts Norm Thagard, Shannon Lucid and John Blaha, had each been on four space flights prior to visiting Mir. All were members of the NASA astronaut corps since before the space shuttle's maiden voyage in 1981. And all were 10 years his senior.

Linenger, who was to take Blaha's place on Mir, will be the first of a new generation of U.S. astronauts aboard the space outpost. The 41-year-old Navy captain and medical doctor, an astronaut for four years, has only about 11 days space experience from a single shuttle flight in 1994.
"I think it will be a rapid learning curve on Mir," he said. "On the other hand I have had a good experience (training) over in Russia and I feel 100 percent ready to go."

Linenger leaves behind a one-year-old son and his wife, Kathryn, who is expecting their second child in late June. Atlantis is supposed to return to Mir in May to bring him home, but he was aware of the chance he would miss the birth.
"If I miss the actual occasion and come home to two children then that's okay, as long as everything turns out okay," Linenger said.

For a man who lists competitive triathalons, marathons, skiing and scuba diving among his interests, being cooped up in the cramped collection of modules that make up Mir may seem stifling, but Linenger said he thinks he will cope.

"I've read a lot about the Antarctic expeditions and living in isolation," he said. "I think running on the treadmill is something I need to do for my bone structure and muscle structure, and for my mental health."
Linenger will not spend his spare time reading books as Lucid did or watching videos like Blaha. Instead he will carry maps and charts to identify the region of earth below him.

"Home is always out the window so I can always look down at earth," he said. "More than just looking out the window, it's a bit of self development trying to be the best geographer in the world would be my goal up there."
Joining Linenger aboard Atlantis will be mission commander Mike Baker, copilot Brent Jett, and mission specialists Jeff Wisoff, Marsha Ivins, and John Grunsfeld.
Meanwhile, John Blaha was ready to come home after four months on the Mir.
"John Blaha has his bags packed and is sitting on his suitcases," said Frank Culbertson, who head's NASA's shuttle-Mir programme. "He's done an excellent job."
